articles.title: Google's Antigravity Remote Agents mean the agent works while you sleep - here's what that actually changes
articles.excerpt: Google's Antigravity v2.29 shipped this week, and the official account confirmed the headline feature is rolling out now: Remote Agents, agent sessions that run in isolated, Google-managed cloud VMs i…
articles.body: Google's Antigravity v2.29 shipped this week, and the official account confirmed the headline feature is rolling out now: Remote Agents, agent sessions that run in isolated, Google-managed cloud VMs instead of on your machine. The marketing line is "fire off a task, step away for coffee, unblock permissions from your phone, and come back to passed tests and a clean PR." The interesting part is not that the agent keeps running while your laptop is closed. It's what that does to the permission model, the trust boundary, and the shape of the work you hand over. I've been waiting for the big tools to make this move, and the details of how Google did it tell you a lot about where agentic development actually is.

articles.title: Budget the Free Tokens Like Cash: One Wallet per Feature
articles.excerpt: Budget the Free Tokens Like Cash: One Wallet per Feature Last month I burned most of a free AI grant in about forty minutes. Not on a big feature. On a retry loop. A summarizer kept returning an empty…
articles.body: Budget the Free Tokens Like Cash: One Wallet per Feature Last month I burned most of a free AI grant in about forty minutes. Not on a big feature. On a retry loop. A summarizer kept returning an empty string. My client retried three times per request. The queue had 900 items. Do the math: roughly 2,700 calls for 900 items, and I was watching the wrong number the whole time. The console showed one number — total tokens. It never told me which feature ate the grant. So I could not separate the runaway loop from real traffic. That was the actual bug. Not the retry. The missing accounting. This post is the fix I now ship first: a per-feature token wallet that fails closed before the call, not after. It is about 90 lines of stdlib Python. No SDK, no database, no dashboard.

articles.body: Most of the AI conversation this week is about whether the tools will replace us, and I keep thinking that the more practical question is whether you can walk away from one. Last month I needed a working vertical slice of a support-triage feature — an HTTP endpoint, one Postgres row, one queued job — and I had an afternoon, not a sprint. So I put the slice on a free tier and it worked, which turned out to be the problem. The demo answered requests beautifully. Then a colleague tried to run it on her machine and we spent three hours working out which parts of that "working" system were actually ours.

articles.title: When a robot misses the stack, which model needs fixing?
articles.excerpt: Suppose a robot reaches for the right block, turns it the wrong way, and misses the target stack. The episode gets a failure mark. That mark doesn't tell you whether the robot chose a bad instruction…
articles.body: Suppose a robot reaches for the right block, turns it the wrong way, and misses the target stack. The episode gets a failure mark. That mark doesn't tell you whether the robot chose a bad instruction or failed to execute a useful one. A hierarchical robot has both a high-level planner, which chooses the next skill and target, and a low-level controller, which moves the arm. Ai2's new ToyBlocks release makes this split testable: either policy level can be replaced by a reference component, called an oracle, while evaluating tasks in the simulated world. [1][2] The useful idea is the controlled replacement, not just another overall success percentage. Computed independent-stage illustration. These are not robot trials, ToyBlocks measurements or named-model scores. Image by the author.

articles.title: Microsoft Entra ID Security: Why Revoking Sessions Isn't Enough
articles.excerpt: 🔐 Microsoft 365 Security: Revoking Sessions Is Not the Same as Blocking User Access An employee leaves the organisation, or their Microsoft 365 account is compromised. As an administrator, you go to…
articles.body: 🔐 Microsoft 365 Security: Revoking Sessions Is Not the Same as Blocking User Access An employee leaves the organisation, or their Microsoft 365 account is compromised. As an administrator, you go to Microsoft Entra ID → Users → Select User → Revoke Sessions . The portal displays a successful message. But here is an important question: Has the user's access actually been terminated? Not necessarily. This is where many administrators need to understand the difference between session revocation and account disablement. Let's break it down. 👇 1️⃣ Revoke Sessions – What actually happens? When you select Revoke Sessions , Microsoft Entra ID invalidates the user's refresh tokens and browser session cookies. This forces supported clients to reauthenticate when they next need a valid session.

articles.body: Twenty tasks. That is the smallest suite I would trust to decide whether a team standardizes on a free AI coding stack — and most teams that ask me the question have zero. Here is a pattern I keep hearing from platform leads (a composite, not one company): a free tier lands, someone runs three prompts against their own repo, two diffs look fine, and a Slack thread turns into a proposal. Then a manager asks the only question that matters — "what breaks if we're wrong?" — and nobody has a number. So let's get the number first. Not a benchmark score from a vendor blog. A pass rate measured on your repo, with your tests as the grader. The decision is a substitution decision, not a price decision You are not buying tokens.

articles.excerpt: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid, the first space rock system "punched" by humanity.
articles.body: The Didymos binary asteroid system, as seen by Europe's Hera probe. The main asteroid, Didymos, dominates the frame while just a sliver of its "moonlet," Dimorphos, is visible beneath it. ESA released this image on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: ESA) The European Space Agency 's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it. The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.

articles.body: The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) . If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho. What is happening? The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun , a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space.

articles.title: 4-billion-year-old 'Rosetta Stone' found in Sahara Desert could unlock the secret history of water on Mars
articles.excerpt: A rock discovered in the Sahara Desert formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, making it one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found. The ancient space rock offers a rare glimpse into the formatio…
articles.body: A rose-colored rock discovered in the Sahara Desert may hold some clues to Mars' ancient geological history. The meteorite , named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered in 2022, weighs roughly 1.8 pounds (800 grams) and formed more than 4.1 billion years ago. Blasted off Mars by an impact before eventually landing on Earth, it is one of the three oldest Martian meteorites ever found. The extraordinary age and unusual mineral composition of Teghaza 001 offer a rare glimpse into the formation of Mars' early crust and how volcanic materials may have been altered by water, according to a statement from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
